map.name: script
map.takes: the command line that runs this file
map.gives: a ready module, and the run of main() when the file is the program
map.text: script — loads the tools this decompiler needs, holds the prompt text that asks Claude to explain one block, and starts main() when the file runs as a program

children.text:
Tools this file needs:
ast — reads Python source as a tree, so the code can find statements, functions and calls
json — reads the answers Claude sends back and writes the map file
re — text patterns
subprocess — runs the claude command as a child program
sys — the command line arguments and the exit path
Path — the source file and the output file as path objects

jedi — finds where each name is defined and where it is used, which becomes the links between texts

PROMPT = the full text of the question sent to Claude for one block.

It holds empty slots that get filled per block: the file name and its numbered lines, the block label and its line ranges, the meanings of the functions this block calls, the list of cells, and the statement ranges.

After the slots come the rules: how the beats must cover the cells in order, how a beat must speak, how the root line must give the signature — and last one example answer, so Claude returns the exact JSON shape the code expects.

CALLS = a counter of the questions sent to Claude, held in a one-item list.

The list makes the count writable from inside ask_claude without a global statement, and the final report prints it.
When this file runs as the program, and not when another file imports it, call main() to read the source file named on the command line, explain every block of it, and write map.json beside it.

map.name: statements
map.takes: a file path and the source text of that file
map.gives: one row per statement: its nesting depth and its line range
map.text: statements(path, src) -> list of (depth, first line, last line) — lists every statement in a python file with the line range it covers and how deep it is nested

children.text:
Take the file path and its source text, and give back an empty list at once when the file is not a .py file.

The statement rows come from the python syntax tree, so a file of another language has nothing to report here.

rows = the collected statements, empty at the start.
Each row it will hold is a triple: the nesting depth, the first line, the last line.
Parse the source into a syntax tree and give the root of that tree to walk() at depth 0; walk() descends the whole tree and appends every statement it meets into rows.
Hand rows back to the caller: the full statement list of the file, in the order the tree was walked.

map.name: statements.walk
map.takes: a syntax node and the nesting depth it sits at
map.gives: nothing; it fills the rows list as it goes
map.text: walk(node, depth) -> nothing — descends one syntax node and appends every statement it meets to rows, tagged with how deep it sits

children.text:
walk takes one syntax node and the depth that node sits at, and looks at each of its direct children in turn.

depth = how many statements this node is nested inside, so every statement found under it can be tagged with its level.

A child that is a statement is one row of the answer: record (depth, its first line, its last line) in rows, then walk into that child with depth + 1, because whatever sits inside a statement is one level deeper than it.

A child that is not a statement — a test, a call, a name — carries no level of its own, so walk steps into it at the same depth. This is how a statement buried under expression nodes still reaches rows with the right number.

map.name: cells_of
map.takes: a file path, its source text, and its lines
map.gives: the cells of the file, each one line range, in file order
map.text: cells_of(path, src, lines) -> list of cells — cuts the whole file into cells, the smallest line ranges a text can be written about, so that every non-blank line sits in exactly one cell

children.text:
spans = the line ranges found so far, empty at the start.

A Python file gets the syntax tree treatment that follows; any other file falls through to the plain-text split below.
Walk the top-level statements of the parsed file and give each one to emit(), which cuts that node into spans: the lines the node owns itself, plus the spans of every statement under it.
If spans is still empty — the file is not Python, or the parse gave nothing — split the raw text instead: each run of non-blank lines becomes one cell, and the function hands those cells back here.

covered = every line number the spans already hold.
extra = the runs of non-blank lines that no span holds.

The tree walk only reports statements, so comments and other lines between them stay unclaimed, and a cell list with holes in it cannot cover the file.

Attach each leftover run to the span that starts after it, by pulling that span's start line up to the start of the run; if no span comes after, stretch the last span down to the end of the run. After this step no line is left out.
Hand back the spans in line order, each one wrapped as a cell record with its single line range.

map.name: cells_of.kids_of
map.takes: one syntax tree node
map.gives: the statement nodes it holds
map.text: kids_of(node) -> list of statement nodes — finds the statement nodes directly under a node, looking through non-statement wrappers

children.text: out = the statement nodes found under this node

Walk the direct children of the node and sort each one:

a child that is a statement — keep it, it is one of the node's own steps

a child that is not a statement, like a test expression or an argument list — call kids_of on it and take the statements from inside, because a statement can hide under a wrapper that is not itself a statement.
So the result is the first layer of real statements, at whatever depth they sit.
hand the collected statement nodes back to the caller

map.name: cells_of.emit
map.takes: one syntax tree node
map.gives: new line spans appended to the shared spans list
map.text: emit(node) -> nothing — cuts one syntax tree node into spans: the lines the node owns itself, plus, through recursion, the spans of every statement under it

children.text:
emit takes one syntax tree node and writes what it finds into the shared spans list.
kids = the statement nodes directly under this node, from kids_of.
A node with no statement under it is a leaf: its full line range becomes one span, and emit stops here.

covered = every line number that a child statement holds.

The same loop calls emit on each child, so each child cuts its own spans one layer down.

Now walk the lines of the node itself and keep only the lines that no child holds:
own = true when line n is outside covered and is not blank.
a = the first line of the run that is open.

Each time a run of own lines ends, it goes into spans. These runs are the lines of the node that its children do not show, such as the "for" line above its body.
If a run is still open at the last line of the node, close it at that line and add it too.

map.name: merge
map.takes: a list of [start, end] line ranges, in any order
map.gives: the same lines as ranges that do not touch each other
map.text: merge(spans) -> list of spans — folds a pile of [start, end] line ranges into the fewest ranges that still cover the same lines

children.text:
The block gets ranges collected from many places, so the same lines can arrive in two ranges that overlap or sit side by side. It hands back one clean list.

out = the finished ranges so far, in order from left to right

Walk the ranges in sorted order, so each one meets the last finished range in out.

If the new start a is no more than one past the end of that last range, the two belong together: stretch the last range's end to whichever end reaches further.
If a sits further away than that, there is a real gap, so the range enters out as a new range of its own.

The + 1 is what makes ranges that only touch, like 5-7 and 8-9, join as well: between line 7 and line 8 there is nothing to leave out.
Hand out back: the same lines, held in the smallest number of ranges.

map.name: ask_claude
map.takes: the full prompt text
map.gives: the parsed JSON answer as a dict
map.text: ask_claude(prompt) -> dict — sends one prompt to the claude command line tool and gives back the JSON object it answered with

children.text:
This is the one door to the model: every block that needs an explanation goes through here with its prompt.

The first act is to add one to CALLS[0], the module-level counter, so the run can report at the end how many times it paid for a model call.

r = the finished claude command, run as a child process with the prompt on the command line and --output-format json so the answer comes back machine-readable.

The call waits up to 600 seconds. Right after it, the assert stops the whole run if claude exited with an error, and shows the last 500 characters of its error output, because a silent failure here would poison every text that follows.

raw = the model's own answer, dug out of the "result" field of the wrapper JSON that the claude tool prints around it.

That answer may still carry stray words before or after the object, so the last line cuts from the first "{" to the last "}" and parses only that slice — the caller gets a plain dict, never text it has to clean up itself.

map.name: check_block
map.takes: the model's answer, plus the block's cells, its statements and its essential lines
map.gives: the accepted root object and beat list
map.text: check_block(m, cells, stmts, ess, label) -> (root, beats) — tests one answer from the model and rejects it with a clear message unless the root fields are complete and the beats cover every cell in order without cutting a statement

children.text:
check_block is the gate between the model and the map: a bad answer must fail here with a message the model can repair, not later as a broken map.

root = the "root" object of the answer, the one line that speaks for the whole block.
If the answer holds no root object, stop immediately.

The root must carry three fields, and each one must be a text with content in it:
text — the signature line and the clause that tells what the block does
takes — the name of the input
gives — the name of the output

When the block is a function, label ends with "()", and then the root text must start with that same name and an open bracket.

This keeps the root a signature of this block, and not a sentence about other code. The top-level script block has no such label, thus it does not get this test.

beats = the list of steps that must tell the story of the block.
An answer with no beats, or with a beats field that is not a list, is rejected.

at = the cell number at which the next beat must start.
It starts at cell 1 and moves forward as the loop goes through the beats.

Go through the beats in order, and test each beat three times:
its first cell is exactly at, thus no cell is missed and no cell is used two times
its last cell b is not before its start and not after the final cell
its text is a string with content in it

got = all the line numbers that the cells of this beat hold, kept only where they agree with ess, the essential lines.

Blank lines and the lines that only open a larger statement are not in ess. Thus they cannot cause a failure in the test that comes after.

Compare the beat with each statement of the block: the beat must hold all the lines of the statement, or only lines from inside it, or none of its lines.

This is the test that stops a beat which cuts a loop or a branch in the middle. When it fails, the message gives the line range of the statement and lists the cells that are inside it, thus the model knows which cells to move.
Move at to one cell after the last cell of this beat, ready for the beat that follows.
After the loop, the last beat must end at the last cell. If it does not, part of the block has no text, and the answer is rejected.
Give the caller the root object and the beat list, both now known to be correct.

map.name: carve
map.takes: a line range, the spans to remove from it, and the file lines
map.gives: the leftover line spans, trimmed
map.text: carve(a, b, minus, lines) -> list of [start, end] — cuts the spans in minus out of the line range a..b and gives back the pieces that stay, with blank lines trimmed off each end

children.text:
used = every line number that the minus spans cover.
The caller passes the spans it wants removed; flattening them to a set of line numbers makes the test "is this line taken?" one lookup.

Walk the range a..b one line at a time and collect each unbroken run of free lines into spans.
run holds the first line of the run that is open now, and None when no run is open. The walk goes one step past b so a run that reaches the end still gets closed and appended.

Trim each raw span and keep only the spans that still hold code.
The two while loops pull the start forward past blank lines and pull the end back past blank lines. A span that is all blank collapses and is dropped, so no piece is only white space.
Give the trimmed spans back to the caller.

map.name: blocks_of
map.takes: the file path, its source text, and its lines
map.gives: the blocks of the file, in file order
map.text: blocks_of(path, src, lines) -> list of blocks — cuts the file into the units the decompiler explains: one block per function or class, plus a script block for the code outside them

children.text:
fns = the record of every function and class in the file, each with its dotted name and its line span.

For a Python file, grab() walks the parsed syntax tree and fills this list; for any other file the list stays empty, so the whole file becomes one block later.

Make one block for each function or class.

A function that holds inner functions must not claim their lines, because those inner ones become blocks of their own. So inner collects the spans of every other record that sits inside this one, and carve() cuts them out and gives back the lines the function keeps for itself.

out = the lines of the file that no function or class covers — the imports, the constants, the code at the bottom.

carve() removes all the function spans from the full file range. If something stays, it becomes a block with the name script and no node, which marks it as the top-level code.
Sort the blocks by their first line and hand them back, so the caller reads them in file order.

map.name: blocks_of.grab
map.takes: a syntax tree node and the chain of names that enclose it
map.gives: nothing of its own; it appends the records to fns
map.text: grab(node, scope) -> nothing — walks the whole syntax tree below one node and fills fns with a record for every function and class it finds, each under its dotted name

children.text:
grab(node, scope) = the recursive finder for definitions.
scope is the chain of names it sits inside, so a def written inside another def can be named blocks_of.grab and not just grab.
Step over the direct children of the node, one at a time.

When the child is a function, an async function, or a class:

a = the first line of that definition, decorator lines counted in, because a decorator stands above the def line and belongs to it.

Add one record to fns: the dotted name, which is scope plus the child's own name; the span from a to its last line; and the node itself, kept for later work on its inside.

Then grab goes down into that child with its name pushed onto scope, so anything defined inside it gets the longer dotted name.

When the child is anything else, grab goes down with scope unchanged, because a plain statement adds no name level. This is how a def hidden in an if, a loop, or a with is still found.

map.name: calls_of
map.takes: one block, the file's top-level statements, and the names of every block
map.gives: the names of the blocks it calls, in sorted order
map.text: calls_of(block, body, names) -> list of names — finds which other blocks of the file this one block calls

children.text:
calls_of answers one question about a block: which other blocks of this file does it use?

Its inputs:
block — the block to look inside, with its dotted name and its syntax node
body — the top-level statements of the file, needed when the block is the script block and has no node of its own
names — every block name in the file, the only names that count as a call

Three names set the search up:

skip = the node types that start a block of their own — a function, an async function, a class
the search must not walk into them, because their calls belong to them and not to this block

scope = the parts of the block's own dotted name, empty for the script block
an inner block can see the names its parents can see, so this is the path a bare word is resolved along

out = the set that collects the names found

Choose what to walk, then hand it to scan.
A real function walks its own node. The script block instead walks the top-level statements of body, less the defs and classes, because those lines are other blocks.
scan(t) adds to out the name of every block called under that node.
Give the collected names back in sorted order, so the call list of a block is always the same list.

map.name: calls_of.resolve
map.takes: a bare name as it is written in the code
map.gives: the full dotted block name, or None when no block has that name
map.text: resolve(word) -> full block name or None — turns a bare name written in the code into the dotted name of the block it points at, using the scope the code stands in

children.text:
resolve(word) — word is one plain name as the code writes it, like emit or grab.

calls_of needs this step because the same short name can mean a different function in a different place: an inner def hides an outer def with the same name.

Try the enclosing scopes from the deepest one out to the top level.

k counts down from the full length of scope to 0, so each turn cuts one level off the front of the scope path.
hit = the candidate full name, the kept part of the scope path and the word joined with dots.
The first hit that is in names is the answer.

The count goes down, not up, so the nearest definition wins, which is the rule Python itself follows.

If no prefix made a known name, give back None.

The word is then not a block of this file — a builtin, an import, or a local variable — so the caller must not count it as a call.

map.name: calls_of.scan
map.takes: a syntax tree node
map.gives: nothing back; it adds the block names it finds to the shared set out
map.text: scan(node) -> None — walks the tree under one node and puts into out the name of every block this block calls

children.text:
scan(node) = the walker that searches one node for the names of other blocks.
It gives nothing back: what it finds goes into the shared set out.

Look at each child node in turn, and step over a child that is a function or a class.
skip holds those node types. The calls inside a nested function belong to that function's own block, not to this one, so scan() must not count them here.

When the child is a bare name in the code, give it to resolve() to find which block that name points at.

hit = the full dotted name of that block, or None when no block has that name.

Keep only a hit that is a different block: a name that points back at this block is not a call out to another block.
Go down into the child with scan() itself, so names deep inside conditions, loops and expressions are found too.

map.name: layers_of
map.takes: the list of blocks and the names each block calls
map.gives: one layer number for each block name
map.text: layers_of(blocks, calls) -> dict from block name to layer number — gives every block a depth number, so a block always sits above the blocks it calls

children.text:
layers_of prepares the tables that the walk over the call graph fills:

idx = the visit number given to each block
low = the lowest visit number each block can reach
on = the blocks that are still on the stack
st = the stack of blocks in visit order
comp = the ring name given to each block

k = a one-item list that holds the next visit number
It is a list, and not a plain number, because strong() must change it from inside.

Call strong() on every block that no earlier walk touched.
When this loop ends, comp holds the answer: blocks that call each other in a circle share one ring name, and a block in no circle is a ring of one.

edges = the calls between rings, and not between single blocks

Look at every call from a block, and keep it only when the two blocks are in different rings. Calls inside one ring go away, thus the ring graph has no circles and a depth is possible to measure.

h = the height already measured for each ring

Measure each ring with height(), and give each block the height of its own ring as its layer number. A block that calls nothing gets layer 1, and each caller gets a higher number than everything below it.

map.name: layers_of.strong
map.takes: the name of one block
map.gives: nothing; it fills idx, low, st, on and comp for v and for every block below it
map.text: strong(v) -> None — visits the block v and every block it can reach, and marks each ring of blocks that call each other with one shared name

children.text:
Stamp v as seen and hold it in the group that is still open:
idx[v] = the visit count, the order in which strong reached v.
low[v] = the smallest visit count that v can reach, which starts as its own count.
k[0] = the next count, ready for the next block.
st = the stack of blocks that have no group yet, with v now on top.
on = the set of the names that are on that stack.

Follow every block that v calls.

A callee with no visit count is new, so strong calls itself on that callee first, then keeps the smaller of low[v] and the callee's low value.
A callee that is already on the stack is part of the same ring, so low[v] keeps the smaller of low[v] and that callee's visit count.

If low[v] is equal to idx[v], no block below v reaches higher than v, thus v is the first block of a ring.
Pop the stack down to v and write comp[w] = v for each block that comes off.
All the blocks of the ring now share one name, v, and the caller can use that ring as one node.

map.name: layers_of.height
map.takes: one component name
map.gives: the height number of that component
map.text: height(c) -> int — measures how many components deep the call chain under a component goes, and remembers the answer

children.text:
height(c) = the depth of the call chain that starts at component c, counted in components.

A component with no outgoing edges has height 1. Any other component is one step taller than the tallest component it calls, so a caller always gets a larger number than everything it depends on. The function asks height() again for each component in edges[c], so the whole chain below c is measured on the way.

Every answer is kept in h, and the work is skipped when c is already in h, so a component shared by many callers is measured one time only. The last line hands back the stored number, for the fresh answer and for the remembered one alike.

map.name: nodes_of
map.takes: a tree of nodes, each node able to hold children
map.gives: a flat list of all the nodes in the tree
map.text: nodes_of(tree) -> list of nodes — flattens a tree of nodes into one list that holds every node, parents and children together

children.text:
out = the flat list that collects every node of the tree.
The callers of nodes_of want to count or scan all texts at once, so the nesting must go away.

Hand the top-level nodes to walk, which adds each one and everything under it to out, then give out back.
Because walk goes down into the children, a node deep in the tree lands in the same list as a node at the top.

map.name: nodes_of.walk
map.takes: a list of tree nodes
map.gives: nothing; it fills the out list of nodes_of
map.text: walk(ns) -> None — adds every node in a list of sibling nodes, and every node under them, to the out list that nodes_of returns

children.text: walk(ns) takes one list of sibling nodes: the whole tree on the first call, and one node's children on every call below that.

Go over the siblings in order and put each node into out, the flat list of nodes that nodes_of gives back.
The order matters: a parent lands in out before anything under it.

When a node has children, walk calls itself on that child list, so the full subtree goes into out directly after its parent.
This recursion is what makes the flat list hold the deep nodes too, not only the top row.

map.name: number
map.takes: the map tree, a list of block roots with children below them
map.gives: nothing; it writes the ids into the nodes it is given
map.text: number(tree) -> nothing — writes an id into every node of the map tree, so each text has a name the reader can point at

children.text:
go through the top nodes of the tree — the block roots — one at a time, in the order they stand in the file.
The count starts at 1, so the first root is number one.

t["id"] = the id of this root: the letter F and the position of the root in two digits, F01, F02, and on.
The two digits keep all ids the same width, so they sort and line up.

k = a counter in a one-item list, set to zero for this root.
It stays outside walk, so each child of this root takes the next number from one shared count.

give the children of the root to walk, which puts a dotted id under the root id on every node below it, F01.1, F01.2, and deeper.
A root with no children becomes an empty list, so there is nothing to name.
At the end of the loop each node in the tree has an id, and number gives nothing back.

map.name: number.walk
map.takes: a list of child nodes
map.gives: nothing; it writes an id into each node it touches
map.text: walk(ns) -> nothing — gives every node in a list of children, and every child under it, a dotted id below the top node it belongs to

children.text:
walk = the helper that numbers one list of child nodes.
It is a helper inside number, so it can read t, the top node it works under, and k, the counter that number keeps for that top node.

map.name: owner_of
map.takes: the finished tree of texts
map.gives: a map from every covered line number to the id of the leaf that holds it
map.text: owner_of(tree) -> dict from line number to node id — says which leaf text owns each line of the file

children.text:
owner = the map from a line number to the id of the text that owns that line.
The reader and the link pass need to go the other way, from a line back to its text, so this pass turns the tree inside out.

Walk every node with nodes_of, but keep only the leaves — a node with no children.
A parent holds the same lines as its children, so only the deepest text is the true owner of a line.
For each leaf, open its line ranges and mark every single line inside them with that leaf's id.
Hand the finished line-to-id map back.

map.name: links
map.takes: the source file path and a map from line number to owning text id
map.gives: one row per shared name: its name, the text that defines it, and the texts that use it
map.text: links(path, owner) -> list of link rows — finds each name defined in this file and reports which other texts use it, so a reader can jump from a use to the place the name is made

children.text: links(path, owner) works on Python only. jedi can read the names out of a .py file and out of nothing else, so any other file gets an empty list back and the map holds no links.

Prepare the three things the search needs:

p = the file path in absolute form, the same form jedi reports for the home file of a name, so the two can be compared

script = a jedi view of the file, which can list the names in it and find every reference to one of them

rows = the empty list that collects one entry per name worth a link
Go through every name jedi finds in the file. Each definition d is one candidate for a link.
Drop the borrowed names. If d points to a place in a different file, the name comes from a library or an import, and this file holds no text that defines it, so it cannot be the target of a link.

src = the id of the text that owns the line where d is defined.

If no text owns that line, there is no place for the link to go, so let the name go by.

used = the ids of the other texts that mention d, in order.

jedi lists every reference to the name inside the file, each reference line becomes the id of the text that owns it, and src itself is kept out because a text does not link to itself.
A name that is used only where it is defined gives no link, so keep a row only when used is not empty. The row holds the name, the text that defines it, and the texts that use it.
Give rows back: all the name links of the file, ready for the reader to make each use clickable.

map.name: row_of
map.takes: a cell number, the cell, and the file lines
map.gives: one printable line for the cell
map.text: row_of(i, c, lines) -> string — writes one cell as a numbered line that the prompt shows to Claude

children.text:
spans = the cell's line ranges as text, like "351-351", joined by commas

A cell can hold more than one range, so every range must appear.

give back one line: the cell number, its ranges, then the first line of code in the cell with the indent removed.

Claude sees this line and picks the cell by its number, so the line must carry both the number and enough code to know the cell.

map.name: write_node
map.takes: a node of the map tree and the indent string for its level
map.gives: the node as a JSON object in text form
map.text: write_node(t, ind) -> string — writes one map node, and its whole subtree under it, as indented JSON text

children.text:
head = the start of the node's JSON object, opened with the indent and the node id.
The block builds the text by hand, and not with json.dumps on the whole node, because the fields must stay in this order and on these lines.

Add the fields that only a block root holds, or the one field a beat holds:

a root node (it has a name) gets name, layer, calls, takes and gives

a beat node gets only its layer

Add the two fields that every node holds: its text and its line ranges.
ensure_ascii=False keeps the accents and the dashes of the text as they are.
A node with no children is complete: close the object and give the text back.

For a node with children, write_node calls itself on each child with two more spaces of indent, joins the children into a list, and closes the parent around them.
Thus the tree shows its depth as indentation in the file.

map.name: write_map
map.takes: the output file path and the finished map object
map.gives: nothing; the map file is written to disk
map.text: write_map(path, m) -> None — writes the whole map — the file name, the links, the terms, and the block tree — to disk as one JSON file laid out for a human to read

children.text:
links_part = the links list as JSON text, one link per line inside brackets

Each link is dumped on its own with ensure_ascii off, so accented words stay readable, and the pieces are joined with a newline and an indent. When there are no links the part is the empty pair "[]", so the file never holds an empty block of whitespace.

terms_part = the terms list as JSON text, in the same one-per-line shape

Same treatment as the links: one term per line, or "[]" when the map has no terms.

tree = the block roots as JSON text, one root after the other

Each root goes through write_node with a four-space indent, which brings its whole subtree of beats down with it, so the tree part is already the full nested map.

Glue the four parts — the file name, links_part, terms_part, and tree — into one JSON object and write it to path.

The braces, keys, and newlines are spelled out by hand instead of letting json.dumps format the whole object, because that is the only way to get this layout: short rows on one line each, the tree nested and indented.

map.name: compile_block
map.takes: one block, its cells, and the file facts the prompt needs
map.gives: the finished tree node for the block: a root plus a child for each beat
map.text: compile_block(bl, cells, name, code, lines, stmts, ess, ctx) -> tree node — writes the prompt for one block, asks Claude again and again until an answer passes the checker, and gives back that block's root text with one child text per beat

children.text:
bstmts = the statements of the file that sit fully inside this block's lines.
stext = a short text that lists those statements as line ranges, a child indented under its parent.

It stays empty when the block holds no statement. Claude gets this outline because a beat must hold all of a statement or none of it.

Make the parts that the prompt template needs:

label — the function name with () after it, or the words for the top-level script code
span — the block's line ranges as one text
rows — one numbered line for each cell, written by row_of

base = the PROMPT template with all of these put in, together with the numbered file, the cell count, and ctx, the one-line meanings of the functions this block calls.

Set up the three values that the retry loop carries:

note — the extra text that goes after the prompt when an answer was bad, empty at the start
errs — every rule that the model broke until now
m — the last answer, still None before the first try

Try eight times at the most. Each try sends the prompt with ask_claude, then gives the answer to check_block, which refuses it unless the root fields are complete and the beats cover all the cells in order without a cut statement.

node = the tree node for the block: the root text, takes and gives, and all the block's cell lines put together by merge.

If the block has more than one cell, each beat becomes a child node at layer 1, and merge again folds the lines of the cells in that beat. Print how many cells became how many beats, then give the node back. This is the good exit from the loop.

If the answer is bad, catch the failure instead of stopping the run. Print the retry, put the message in errs, and make note, which shows Claude its last answer, the rule it broke, and all the rules it broke before, and asks for the full corrected JSON. The next try sends base and note together.
Eight bad answers one after the other stop everything: sys.exit ends the compile and names the block that did not pass.

map.name: main
map.takes: a source file path on the command line
map.gives: a map.json file beside that source file
map.text: main() -> None — reads the file named on the command line, explains every block of it, and writes the result to map.json

children.text:
main() is the whole run: it takes one file path on the command line and explains that file.

path = the file to explain, taken from sys.argv[1]
src = the text of that file
lines = that text cut into single lines

The assert stops the run at once when the file holds no text, because there is nothing to explain.

code = the same file with a line number and a bar in front of every line
Every prompt shows the file in this form, so a text can speak about lines by their number.

Cut the file two ways, because the prompts and the checker need different pieces:

cells — cells_of gives the smallest line ranges a text can be written about
stmts — statements gives every statement of the file with its nesting depth and its line range

ess = the lines that a beat is not permitted to cut through
Only the innermost statements count: a statement that holds another statement inside it is left out, and the blank lines are removed at the end. The checker in check_block uses this set to test that a beat holds all of a statement or none of it.

Find the blocks of the file and put them in order of depth:

blocks — blocks_of cuts the file into one block for each function or class, plus a script block
body — the top-level statements of the file, which calls_of needs for the script block
names — the name of every block that is a function or a class
calls — calls_of gives, for each block, the names of the blocks it calls
lay — layers_of turns those calls into one layer number for each block, so a block always sits above the blocks it calls

parts = the cells of each block, kept under the name of the block
Each cell goes to the one block whose line ranges contain it. Thus each block is explained from its own cells only.

Explain the blocks from the bottom up: the loop takes them in layer order, thus every block that a block calls is already explained before that block starts.

For each block it makes ctx, the one-line meanings of the callees that are already in done, and gives ctx and the block's cells to compile_block. compile_block gives back the root node with one child for each beat. main() then writes the name, the layer, the calls and the block's line ranges into that node and keeps it in done.

Put the finished roots in file order and prepare them for the reader:

tree = all the block roots, sorted by their first line
number writes an id into every node of the tree
owner = owner_of, which says which leaf text owns each line of the file

m = the full map object: the file name, the cross-references that links finds with the help of owner, an empty terms list, and the tree
write_map writes m to map.json in the same folder as the source file.
Print the counts — blocks, texts, links, Claude calls — and the path of the file that was written, so the person who started the run sees what was made and what it cost.
